title: How did 168 conquistadors take down the Inca empire?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how a Spanish force of about 168 conquistadors led by Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca empire in the 1530s. They cover the Inca state's rapid expansion, its rigid class system and bureaucracy, and its use of divide-and-conquer and cultural dilution to rule conquered peoples. They describe the fracturing caused by the Huascar–Atahualpa civil war, the advantages of guns and the belief that the Spanish were returning gods, Atahualpa's capture and execution, the puppet ruler Manco Inca's revolt and the Vilcabamba state, and the 1572 death of Túpac Amaru. Smallpox, which spread ahead of the Spanish and devastated Andean populations, is presented as a key factor. The episode opens with a Co-ED scholarship sponsor shout-out and includes a listener mail about GPS replacing sextants in Coast Guard navigation.

segments.title: Opening ad and Co-ED sponsorship plug
segments.summary: Opens with a Toyota Corolla ad, then the hosts promote Co-ED's Guatemala scholarship program and read names of new scholarship sponsors.

segments.title: Introduction and cultural relativism banter
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the Inca topic and discuss cultural relativism, including Josh's changed view and a Facebook exchange about Alan Turing's posthumous pardon.

segments.title: Inca child sacrifice and cultural context
segments.summary: The hosts describe Inca child sacrifice as rare, ritualized and revered, mostly reserved for dire circumstances, and debate whether it fits cultural relativism.

segments.title: Inca rise, technology and class system
segments.summary: The Inca grew to about a million people in a couple of centuries, using irrigation, terracing and crops such as potatoes. Their rigid class system and incestuous royal line are described.

segments.title: Inca expansion, roads, runners and bureaucracy
segments.summary: The Inca expanded by force or persuasion, used cultural dilution by relocating peoples, and ran a large bureaucracy. A correction notes that runners worked in relays covering 250 miles a day.

segments.title: Inca civil war and the conquest begins
segments.summary: The deaths of Huayna Capac and his successor led to a seven-year civil war between Huascar and Atahualpa, which Atahualpa won. Pizarro arrived with fewer than 200 men, inspired by Cortes's success against the Aztecs.

segments.title: Capture of Atahualpa and puppet rule
segments.summary: Guns, the belief that the Spanish were returning gods, and Atahualpa's capture allowed Pizarro to take power. Atahualpa was executed, and Manco Inca was installed as puppet ruler before fleeing to found Vilcabamba.

segments.title: Tupac Amaru's death and smallpox
segments.summary: Vilcabamba fell in 1572 and Tupac Amaru was beheaded, ending the Inca state. Smallpox, which the Spanish unknowingly carried, killed Huayna Capac and devastated populations, and the hosts estimate 90 to 95 percent of Indigenous Americans died within about 130 years.
